title: Copies of Copies, Doubling Each Cycle

scenes.tts: Put ten molecules of DNA in a tube. Thirty rounds of copying can turn them into about ten billion. No living cell is involved. How does a tube of DNA do that? And why does a real reaction stop short?
scenes.visual: Ten duplexes in a tube; arrow of thirty rounds to a dense field labelled about ten billion; crossed-out cell; question marks over a stop line.
scenes.narration: Put ten molecules of DNA in a tube. Thirty rounds of copying can turn them into about ten billion. No living cell is involved. How does a tube of DNA do that? And why does a real reaction stop short?

scenes.tts: The trick is two short primers. A primer pairs with the template and gives the polymerase a place to start. The two primers bind opposite strands, one on each side of the region to copy. Polymerase can only add to the three prime end of a primer. So the primers must point toward each other, three prime ends facing in.
scenes.caption: The trick is two short primers. A primer pairs with the template and gives the polymerase a place to start. The two primers bind opposite strands, one on each side of the region to copy. Polymerase can only add to the 3' end of a primer. So the primers must point toward each other, 3' ends facing in.
scenes.visual: Template duplex with 5' and 3' ends; two yellow primer arrows pair on opposite strands, 3' ends pointing inward, extension arrows between them.
scenes.narration: The trick is two short primers. A primer pairs with the template and gives the polymerase a place to start. The two primers bind opposite strands, one on each side of the region to copy. Polymerase can only add to the 3' end of a primer. So the primers must point toward each other, 3' ends facing in.

scenes.tts: Each cycle has three steps. First, heat the tube to about ninety-four to ninety-eight degrees Celsius, and the two strands separate. Second, cool the tube a few degrees below the primers' melting temperature. Each primer pairs with its site. Third, typically at seventy-two degrees for Tack polymerase, each primer is lengthened from five prime to three prime.
scenes.caption: Each cycle has three steps. First, heat the tube to about 94 to 98 °C, and the two strands separate. Second, cool the tube a few degrees below the primers' melting temperature. Each primer pairs with its site. Third, typically at 72 °C for Taq polymerase, each primer is lengthened from 5' to 3'.
scenes.visual: Three step chips light in turn; strands pull apart, primers pair, blue new DNA grows from each primer.
scenes.narration: Each cycle has three steps. First, heat the tube to about 94 to 98 °C, and the two strands separate. Second, cool the tube a few degrees below the primers' melting temperature. Each primer pairs with its site. Third, typically at 72 °C for Taq polymerase, each primer is lengthened from 5' to 3'.

scenes.tts: In cycle one, copies start at a primer but run past the other site. Because the primers face each other, each new strand contains a site for the other primer. So the products of one cycle become templates for the next. It is like a photocopier whose copies can be copied. Molecules bounded by both primers first appear in cycle three. After three cycles, two of the eight are exact length. By cycle thirty, they are nearly all of the product.
scenes.visual: One duplex becomes two, four, eight rows; new strands grow from the primer sites; in cycle three the two exact-length duplexes turn green.
scenes.narration: In cycle one, copies start at a primer but run past the other site. Because the primers face each other, each new strand contains a site for the other primer. So the products of one cycle become templates for the next. It is like a photocopier whose copies can be copied. Molecules bounded by both primers first appear in cycle three. After three cycles, two of the eight are exact length. By cycle thirty, they are nearly all of the product.

scenes.tts: Doubling is what makes this powerful. With perfect doubling, each cycle multiplies the number of copies by two. Thirty cycles multiply it by two to the thirtieth power, which is just over one billion. Ten molecules become about ten billion.
scenes.caption: Doubling is what makes this powerful. With perfect doubling, each cycle multiplies the number of copies by two. Thirty cycles multiply it by 2 to the 30th power, which is just over one billion. Ten molecules become about ten billion.
scenes.visual: Cycle counter runs 0 to 30 while the copy number climbs from 10 to 10,737,418,240.
scenes.narration: Doubling is what makes this powerful. With perfect doubling, each cycle multiplies the number of copies by two. Thirty cycles multiply it by 2 to the 30th power, which is just over one billion. Ten molecules become about ten billion.

scenes.tts: A real reaction stops short. Amplification is exponential only in the early cycles. Then it slows and reaches a plateau. In one model system, reactions with different starting amounts reached the same final level. So a bright band at the end does not tell you how much DNA you began with. Each cycle doubles the copies, but only early on.
scenes.visual: Three curves from different starts climb steeply, bend, and merge on one plateau; note that the endpoint does not reveal the start.
scenes.narration: A real reaction stops short. Amplification is exponential only in the early cycles. Then it slows and reaches a plateau. In one model system, reactions with different starting amounts reached the same final level. So a bright band at the end does not tell you how much DNA you began with. Each cycle doubles the copies, but only early on.
